In [[mathematics]], '''pseudo-Zernike polynomials''' are well known and widely used in the analysis of [[optics|optical]] systems. They are also widely used in [[image analysis]] as [[Shape analysis (digital geometry)#Shape descriptors|shape descriptors]].

== Definition ==
They are an [[orthogonal]] set of [[complex number|complex]]-valued [[polynomials]]
defined as

:<math>
V_{nm}(x,y) = R_{nm}(x,y)e^{jm\arctan(\frac{y}{x})},
</math>

where <math>x^2+y^2\leq 1, n\geq 0, |m|\leq n</math> and orthogonality on the [[unit disk]] is given as

:<math>
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r [V_{nl}(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)]^* \times
                            V_{mk}(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,dr\,d\theta =
                            \frac{\pi}{n+1}\delta_{mn}\delta_{kl},
</math>

where the star means complex conjugation, and
<math>
r^2 = x^2+y^2</math>, <math>x=r\cos\theta</math>, <math>y=r\sin\theta
</math>
are the standard transformations between polar and Cartesian coordinates.

The radial polynomials <math>R_{nm}</math> are defined as<ref name=Teh88 />

<math>
R_{nm}(r) = \sum_{s=0}^{n-|m|}D_{n,|m|,s}\ r^{n-s}
</math>

with integer coefficients

:<math>
D_{n,|m|,s} = (-1)^s\frac{(2n+1-s)!}{s!(n-|m|-s)!(n+|m|-s+1)!}.
</math>

==Examples==
Examples are:
<!--
# Maple
Dzer := proc(n,m,s)
        (-1)^s * (2*n+1-s)!/s!/(n-abs(m)-s)!/(n+abs(m)-s+1)! ;
end proc:
R := proc(n,m,r)
        add( Dzer(n,m,s)*r^(n-s),s=0..n-abs(m)) ;
end proc:
for n from 0 to 5 do
        for m from 0 to n do
                # print(n,m, R(n,m,r) ) ;
                printf("<math>") ;
                printf("R_{%d,%d} = %a",n,m,R(n,m,r) ) ;
                printf("</math>\n\n") ;
        end do:
end do:
-->

<math>R_{0,0} = 1</math>

<math>R_{1,0} = -2+3 r</math>

<math>R_{1,1} = r</math>

<math>R_{2,0} = 3+10 r^2-12 r</math>

<math>R_{2,1} = 5 r^2-4 r</math>

<math>R_{2,2} = r^2</math>

<math>R_{3,0} = -4+35 r^3-60 r^2+30 r</math>

<math>R_{3,1} = 21 r^3-30 r^2+10 r</math>

<math>R_{3,2} = 7 r^3-6 r^2</math>

<math>R_{3,3} = r^3</math>

<math>R_{4,0} = 5+126 r^4-280 r^3+210 r^2-60 r</math>

<math>R_{4,1} = 84 r^4-168 r^3+105 r^2-20 r</math>

<math>R_{4,2} = 36 r^4-56 r^3+21 r^2</math>

<math>R_{4,3} = 9 r^4-8 r^3</math>

<math>R_{4,4} = r^4</math>

<math>R_{5,0} = -6+462 r^5-1260 r^4+1260 r^3-560 r^2+105 r</math>

<math>R_{5,1} = 330 r^5-840 r^4+756 r^3-280 r^2+35 r</math>

<math>R_{5,2} = 165 r^5-360 r^4+252 r^3-56 r^2</math>

<math>R_{5,3} = 55 r^5-90 r^4+36 r^3</math>

<math>R_{5,4} = 11 r^5-10 r^4</math>

<math>R_{5,5} = r^5</math>

==Moments==
The pseudo-Zernike Moments (PZM) of order <math>n</math> and repetition <math>l</math> are defined as

:<math>
A_{nl}=\frac{n+1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 [V_{nl}(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)]^*
f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta,
</math>

where <math>n = 0, \ldots \infty</math>, and <math>l</math> takes on positive and negative [[integer]]
values subject to <math>|l|\leq n</math>.

The image function can be reconstructed by expansion of the pseudo-Zernike coefficients on the unit disk as

:<math>
f(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{l=-n}^{+n}A_{nl}V_{nl}(x,y).
</math>

Pseudo-Zernike moments are derived from conventional [[Zernike moments]] and shown
to be more robust and less sensitive to image [[noise]] than the Zernike moments.<ref name="Teh88">{{cite journal
|first1=C.-H.
|last1=Teh
|last2=Chin
|first2=R.
|title=On image analysis by the methods of moments
|journal=IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
|volume=10
|issue=4
|year=1988
|pages=496&ndash;513
|doi=10.1109/34.3913
}}</ref>
